source_text: Est et alius summus impatientiae stimulus ultionis libido, negotium curans aut gloriae aut malitiae. sed et gloria ubique uana et malitia numquam non domino odiosa, hoc quidem loco cum maxime, cum alterius malitia prouocata superiorem se in exsequenda ultione constituit et remunerans nequam duplicat quod semel factum est ultio penes errorem solacium uidetur doloris, penes ueritatem certamen redarguitur malignitatis. quid enim refert inter prouocantem et prouocatum, nisi quod ille prior in maleficio deprehenditur, at ille posterior? tamen uterque laesi hominis domino reus est, qui omne nequam et prohibet et damnat. nulla in maleficio ordinis ratio est, nec locus secernit quod similitudo coniungit. par factum par habet meritum. absolute itaque praecipitur malum malo non rependendum. quomodo id obseruabimus, si fastidientes * in fastidio ultionis non erimus? quem autem honorem litabimus domino deo, ei nobis arbitrium defensionis arrogauerimus? nos putres, uasa fictilia! seruulis nostris adsumentibus sibi de conseruis ultionem grauiter offendimur eosque, qui nobis patientiam obtulerint suam, ut memores humilitatis seruitutis suae, dominici honoris diligentes non probamus modo, sed ampliorem, quam ipsi sibi praesumpsissent, satisfactionem facimus. id nobis in domino tam iusto ad aestimandum, tam potenti ad perficiendum periclitatur? ** hoc se nobis repromittit dicens: uindictam mihi, et ego uindicabo, id est: patientiam tibi, et ego patientiam remunerabo. cum enim dicit: nolite iudicare, ne iudicemini, nonne patientiam flagitat? quis enim non iudicabit alium, nisi qui patiens erit non defendendi? quid ergo credimus iudicem illum, si non et ultorem? quis idcirco iudicat, ut ignoscat? ac si ignoscet, tamen iudicantis impatientiam cauerit et honorem unici iudicis [id est dei] abstulerit. quantos uero casus huiusmodi impatientia incursare consueuit! quotiens paenituit defensionem! quotiens instantia eius deterior inuenta est causis suis! quoniam nihil impatientia susceptum sine impetu transigi nouit, nihil impetu actum non aut offendit aut corruit aut praeceps abit. iam si leuius defenderis, insanies, si uberius, oneraberis. quid mihi cum ultione, cuius modum regere non possum per impatientiam doloris? quodsi patientiae incubabo, non dolebo; si non dolebo, ulcisci non desiderabo.
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that impatience is the root of every sin, and now turns to the desire for revenge as a chief stimulus of impatience.
pass_a_gloss: There is also another chief stimulus of impatience: the desire for revenge, a business that cares for either glory or malice. But glory is everywhere empty, and malice is never not hateful to the Lord, especially in this matter, when, provoked by another's malice, it sets itself up as superior in carrying out revenge, and, repaying the wicked person, doubles what was done once. Revenge, in the case of error, seems a comfort of grief; in the case of truth, it is convicted as a contest of wickedness. For what difference is there between the provoker and the provoked, except that the former is caught first in wrongdoing, and the latter later? Yet each is guilty before the Lord of the injured man, who both forbids and condemns every wicked thing. There is no account of order in wrongdoing, nor does place separate what likeness joins. An equal deed has equal merit. Therefore it is absolutely commanded that evil is not to be repaid with evil. How shall we observe this, if we are not disdainful of revenge in our disdain? What honor shall we offer to the Lord God, if we have arrogated to ourselves the right of defense? We are rotten, earthen vessels! When our slaves take revenge on their fellow slaves, we are gravely offended, and those who have offered us their patience, as mindful of the humility of their servitude, loving the honor of the master, we not only approve, but we make them give a greater satisfaction than they themselves would have presumed. Is this endangered for us in the Lord, who is so just in judging, so powerful in accomplishing? He promises this to us, saying: Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, that is: Patience is yours, and I will repay patience. For when he says: Do not judge, lest you be judged, does he not demand patience? For who will not judge another, except the one who will be patient in not defending himself? What then do we believe that judge to be, if not also an avenger? Who judges for this reason, that he may forgive? And if he will forgive, nevertheless he has avoided the impatience of judging and has taken away the honor of the only judge, that is, of God. How many misfortunes impatience of this kind is accustomed to run into! How often defense has caused regret! How often its urgency has been found worse than its causes! Since impatience knows nothing undertaken without violence to be finished, nothing done with violence does not either offend or collapse or rush headlong away. Now if you defend yourself too lightly, you will rage; if too fully, you will be burdened. What have I to do with revenge, whose measure I cannot control through impatience of grief? But if I shall lie upon patience, I shall not grieve; if I shall not grieve, I shall not desire to take revenge.

choices.why: Keeps the force of libido as strong desire or lust, and ultio as revenge per glossary.

choices.term: negotium curans aut gloriae aut malitiae
choices.english: a business that cares for either glory or malice
choices.why: Preserves the metaphor of revenge as a negotium (business/affair) and the double object of glory or malice.

a pursuit of either glory or malice

choices.why: Literal rendering of the biblical image of human frailty; keeps the plural and the material sense.

choices.english: Vengeance is mine, and I will repay
choices.why: Renders the quoted divine speech literally, preserving the first-person divine claim and the future verb.
rejected: Revenge is mine, I will repay
Mine is vengeance, I will recompense

choices.term: patientiam tibi, et ego patientiam remunerabo
choices.english: Patience is yours, and I will repay patience
choices.why: Keeps the parallel structure Tertullian draws between God's vengeance and the believer's patience, with remunerabo as repay.
rejected: Patience for you, and I will reward patience
Yours is patience, and I will recompense patience

choices.english: Do not judge, lest you be judged
choices.why: Standard literal rendering of the biblical command, preserving the passive subjunctive.
rejected: Judge not, that you be not judged
Stop judging, so that you will not be judged

pass_b_english: There is also another supreme goad of impatience: the desire for revenge, a business that cares for either glory or malice. But glory is always empty, and malice is never anything but hateful to the Lord—especially in this matter, when one person's malice is provoked and sets itself up as superior in carrying out revenge. By repaying a wicked person, it doubles what was done once. Revenge seems to the erring a comfort for grief, but in truth it is exposed as a contest of wickedness. What difference is there between the provoker and the provoked, except that the one is caught first in the evil deed and the other later? Yet both are guilty before the Lord of the wronged man, who both forbids and condemns every wicked thing. There is no order of rank in wrongdoing, and place does not separate what likeness joins. An equal deed has equal merit. So it is absolutely commanded that evil is not to be repaid with evil. How will we observe this if we are not thoroughly disdainful of revenge? What honor will we offer the Lord God if we claim for ourselves the right of defense? We are rotten, earthen vessels! When our slaves take revenge on their fellow slaves, we are gravely offended. Those who offer us their patience, mindful of the humility of their servitude and loving the honor of their master, we not only approve but ourselves make greater satisfaction than they would have presumed for themselves. Does this imperil us before the Lord, who is so just in judging and so powerful in accomplishing? He promises this to us, saying: Vengeance is mine, and I will repay (Romans 12:19; Deuteronomy 32:35)—that is, patience is yours, and I will reward patience. For when he says, Do not judge, lest you be judged (Matthew 7:1), does he not demand patience? Who will not judge another except the one who is patient enough not to defend himself? Do we believe that judge is not also an avenger? Who judges for the purpose of forgiving? And if he does forgive, he has still guarded against the impatience of judging and taken away the honor of the one judge, that is, God. How many disasters impatience of this kind is accustomed to rush into! How often defense has been regretted! How often its insistence has turned out worse than the causes themselves! For impatience knows how to undertake nothing without violence, and nothing done with violence fails to offend, or collapse, or rush headlong away. If you defend yourself too feebly, you will rage; if too fully, you will be burdened. What is revenge to me, whose measure I cannot control through impatience of grief? But if I rest upon patience, I will not grieve; if I do not grieve, I will not desire revenge.
notes: The source contains two asterisks marking possible damage or uncertainty: after 'fastidientes *' and after 'perficiendum periclitatur? **'. The gloss renders the text as it stands without inventing missing words.

problems.quote: we not only approve but make them give greater satisfaction
problems.source_quote: sed ampliorem, quam ipsi sibi praesumpsissent, satisfactionem facimus
problems.why: We ourselves make satisfaction (to God), greater than slaves presumed for themselves; English says we make slaves give it.
problems.fix: we not only approve but ourselves make greater satisfaction than they would have presumed for themselves
problems.ruling: Latin ‘facimus satisfactionem’ means ‘we make a greater satisfaction’, not ‘make them give’; English adds wrong agent.

problems.quote: Is that dangerous for us to do with the Lord
problems.source_quote: id nobis in domino tam iusto ad aestimandum, tam potenti ad perficiendum periclitatur?
problems.why: Subject is 'id' (this claim of self-defense); it imperils us before a Lord so just and powerful, not 'is it dangerous to do with the Lord.'
problems.fix: Does this imperil us before the Lord, so just in judging, so powerful in accomplishing?
problems.ruling: ‘id … periclitatur’ = ‘this endangers us before a Lord…’, not a question ‘Is that dangerous for us to do with the Lord’.

problems.quote: nothing done with violence does not offend, or collapse, or rush headlong away.
problems.source_quote: nihil impetu actum non aut offendit aut corruit aut praeceps abit.
problems.why: English reverses the double negative, implying violence does not cause offense, collapse, or rush, opposite of Latin.
problems.fix: nothing done with violence fails to offend, does not collapse, and does not rush headlong.
problems.ruling: Latin 'nihil...non aut offendit aut corruit' = everything done with violence offends/collapses. English 'nothing...does not' reverses meaning.

edits.old: we not only approve but make them give greater satisfaction than they would have presumed for themselves
edits.new: we not only approve but ourselves make greater satisfaction than they would have presumed for themselves

edits.old: Is that dangerous for us to do with the Lord, who is so just in judging and so powerful in accomplishing?
edits.new: Does this imperil us before the Lord, who is so just in judging and so powerful in accomplishing?

fixed: The English misstates the source: 'satisfactionem facimus' means we ourselves make satisfaction, not that we make slaves give it.
The English misstates the source: 'id nobis in domino... periclitatur' means this thing imperils us before the Lord, not that it is dangerous for us to do with the Lord.
The English reverses the double negative: 'nihil impetu actum non aut offendit aut corruit aut praeceps abit' means nothing done with violence fails to offend, collapse, or rush headlong.

problems.quote: who both forbids and condemns every wicked person
problems.source_quote: qui omne nequam et prohibet et damnat
problems.why: omne nequam is neuter: 'every wicked thing/deed', not 'every wicked person'.
problems.fix: who both forbids and condemns every wicked thing
problems.ruling: "omne nequam" is neuter singular, meaning “every wicked thing,” not “person”

edits.old: who both forbids and condemns every wicked person
edits.new: who both forbids and condemns every wicked thing

fixed: Changed 'every wicked person' to 'every wicked thing' because 'omne nequam' is neuter, referring to every wicked deed or thing, not a person.

problems.quote: if we are not free from disdain for revenge
problems.source_quote: si fastidientes in fastidio ultionis non erimus
problems.why: Latin means 'if we are disdainful, we will not be free from disdain for revenge'; English reverses the logic.
problems.fix: if we are disdainful, we will not be free from disdain for revenge?
problems.ruling: Latin 'si ... non erimus' = 'if we will not be', opposite of English 'if we are not free'

problems.quote: patience is yours, and I will repay patience
problems.source_quote: patientiam tibi, et ego patientiam remunerabo
problems.why: 'Remunerabo' means 'reward', not 'repay'; the contrast is vengeance vs. patience rewarded.
problems.fix: patience is yours, and I will reward patience
problems.ruling: Latin 'remunerabo' = reward; English adds 'patience is yours' and uses 'repay' altering sense

problems.quote: So it is absolutely commanded that evil is not to be repaid with evil (Romans 12:17).
problems.source_quote: absolute itaque praecipitur malum malo non rependendum.
problems.why: The Latin does not cite Romans 12:17; the citation is an addition not in the source.
problems.fix: So it is absolutely commanded that evil is not to be repaid with evil.
problems.ruling: Latin 'absolute itaque praecipitur' has no scripture reference; '(Romans 12:17)' is added, not in source.

fixed.quote: How will we observe this if we are disdainful, we will not be free from disdain for revenge?
fixed.fix: How will we observe this if we are not thoroughly disdainful of revenge?
fixed.note: The English is an ungrammatical run-on. The Latin has a lacuna, but its sense is that we keep the command only by disdaining revenge.
